text:
Leader of the eight Zamfara lawmakers that resigned from the All Progressives Congress (APC) due to alleged injustice, Aliyu Ango Kagara, said he and his colleagues have not taken a final decision on returning to the APC even after meeting with President Bola Ahmed Tinubu.
Daily Trust reported that the eight resigned from the APC in protest but were taken to see the President by the minister of state for defence, Bello Matawalle on Sunday to pave the way for their return to the APC.
Kagara who gave an insight into what transpired at the meeting with the President, said they’re yet to reunite with the APC but had attended a meeting with the president following an invitation to explain their position and the origins of the crisis.
“We were at the Presidential Villa on invitation. Initially, some of us attempted to reject it, but we later agreed to honour the invitation out of respect for the President,” Kagara said.
He added that Tinubu explained that he had invited them to hear their side of the story because he had received different accounts of what transpired.
“The president said he invited us to hear what really transpired because he had heard different versions of the story,” he said.
Kagara reiterated that the lawmakers had not reversed their decision to leave the APC, insisting that they did not tell the president they had returned to the party.
“Even the president knew that we had left the party, and we did not tell him that we had returned,” he said adding that they briefed President Tinubu on what they described as the injustices they had suffered, adding that the President promised to invite the other faction to a meeting with them to find a solution to the crisis.
On the possibility of returning to the APC, Kagara said the decision was beyond the individual lawmakers, stressing that their constituents had a say in the matter.
“Our people have the final say. We are struggling for their voices to be heard,” he said.
He also maintained that their position remained unchanged: the insecurity affecting their constituencies must be addressed decisively.
“The issue of settling our entitlement to return to the APC does not even arise. Initially, we confronted Governor Lawal to sit up and address insecurity, and we are still on that.
“Had it been that we agreed to remain silent on insecurity, we would have been treated equally. But we resisted, and we told Mr President that more needed to be done on the issue of insecurity. He assured us that he would do more. We need our people to survive; payment of our entitlement is just a secondary issue,” he said.
Kagara also accused Governor Dauda Lawal of failing to do what was expected of him to complement the Federal Government’s efforts to tackle insecurity in the state.
He dismissed claims by some members of the state House of Assembly that the government had achieved 89 per cent success in addressing insecurity, describing the figure as false.
“Those members in the State Assembly are just propaganda that the government had achieved 89 per cent on security, which is a blatant lie,” he said.
Kagara further alleged that the state government is not doing enough to address the worsening security situation.
He revealed that President Tinubu had indicated his intention to invite Governor Lawal and the lawmakers to a meeting, adding that this was why they had refrained from making further public comments on the matter.
“Governor Lawal is not doing anything on insecurity, looking at the growing rate of the menace. But the president said he would invite the governor and us. That is why we did not intend to say anything because we do not know what to say about it,” Kagara said.
The State Auditor of the APC and Publicity Secretary of the Matawalle Political Standing Committee, Malam Yusuf Idris Gusau, said the minister took steps to bring the lawmakers before President Bola Tinubu as part of efforts to strengthen the party ahead of the elections.
He said the initiative was aimed at uniting aggrieved party members and creating an opportunity for them to contribute to the APC’s electoral fortunes.
Yusuf Idris described the minister’s engagement with the lawmakers as a significant step towards reconciliation, adding that their appearance in a photograph with a national party leader suggested that discussions had taken place.
